subject: chess computer
title: What If a Machine Beat the World Chess Champion? In 1997 It Took 19 Moves

scenes.text: What if a machine beat the best chess player alive? In 1997 the final game took 19 moves.
Garry Kasparov had been world champion for twelve years. In 1996 he beat IBM's Deep Blue four games to two.
IBM rebuilt it: 256 processors, checking about 200 million chess positions every second. The rematch was in New York, May 1997.
Kasparov won game one. Deep Blue won game two. Three draws followed. Everything came down to game six.
Deep Blue won it in 19 moves. Three and a half to two and a half. A machine had beaten a sitting world champion in a match for the first time.
The prize was 700,000 dollars. The chess app on your phone would beat Deep Blue today. The humans never got the title back.

description:
What if a computer beat the world chess champion? On 11 May 1997 IBM's Deep Blue, a 256-processor machine evaluating about 200 million positions a second, beat Garry Kasparov 3.5 to 2.5 in New York, winning the deciding sixth game in 19 moves.
Kasparov had won the first match in 1996 by 4 to 2. The 1997 rematch carried a 700,000 dollar prize and was the first time a reigning world champion lost a match to a machine under tournament conditions.
